content: The European Pharmacopoeia is a comprehensive compilation of active substances and excipients utilized in the preparation of pharmaceutical products across Europe. The 2005 edition encompasses 1,800 specific and general monographs, which include a variety of chemical substances, antibiotics, biological substances, vaccines for both human and veterinary use, immunosera, radiopharmaceutical preparations, herbal drugs, homeopathic preparations, and homeopathic stocks. Additionally, it provides detailed information on dosage forms, general monographs, materials and containers, and sutures. It describes 268 general methods, often accompanied by figures or chromatograms, and includes 2,210 reagents. The monographs establish quality standards for all major medicines used in Europe. Compliance with these quality standards is mandatory for all medicines sold in the 36 Member States of the European Pharmacopoeia, ensuring that consumers receive products of guaranteed quality from pharmacies and other authorized suppliers. The European Pharmacopoeia is developed by the European Directorate for the Quality of Medicines (EDQM), which operates under the Council of Europe in Strasbourg, France. Its foundation is based on the 1964 Convention on the Elaboration of a European Pharmacopoeia. The EDQM publishes the pharmacopoeia in English and French, with official national translations available in German and Spanish (the Spanish version is available exclusively online). Currently, the European Pharmacopoeia Commission comprises 37 members, including Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Montenegro, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Serbia, Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and the European Union. In these countries and the European Union, the European Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Eur.) serves as the official pharmacopoeia. However, additional local pharmacopoeias may exist, such as those in the United Kingdom and Germany. It is important to note that not all of these countries are members of the European Union. Observers from 20 non-member states and international organizations also participate in the sessions of the European Pharmacopoeia Commission. These observers include Albania, Algeria, Australia, Belarus, Brazil, Canada, China, Georgia, Israel, Madagascar, Malaysia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, the Russian Federation, Senegal, Syria, Tunisia, Ukraine, the United States of America, and the World Health Organization (WHO). The convention is open for signature by all European countries, while other countries may obtain observer status. Since the 5th edition, the pharmacopoeia has been published in two volumes. Volume 1 contains general chapters and monographs, such as those on dosage forms, methods of analysis, and reagents, while Volume 2 includes all substance monographs. During the runtime of the current edition, several supplements are published. Electronic versions are also available, including CD-ROM and online formats. The European Pharmacopoeia is frequently abbreviated as Ph. Eur. and is often referenced in the context of a drug's ingredients.
